turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_htsteel_pareto_train.csv: 300 real steels, process/composition
    columns (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo, Mn, C, Ti, Si, Nb, V, P, B, Al, Cu, W, S, Heat treatment
    step 1 temperature, Heat treatment step 1 time, Heat treatment step 1 cooling rate, Heat treatment step 2
    temperature, Heat treatment step 2 time, Heat treatment step 2 cooling rate, Heat treatment step 3
    temperature, Heat treatment step 3 time, Heat treatment step 3 cooling rate, Secondary treatment step 1
    temperature, Secondary treatment step 1 time, Secondary treatment step 2 temperature, Secondary treatment step 2
    time, Secondary treatment step 3 temperature, Secondary treatment step 3 time, Secondary treatment step 4
    temperature, Secondary treatment step 4 time, Thermal exposure temperature, Thermal exposure time) and
    the two measured objectives `yield strength (MPa)` and `elongation (%)`
    (both at room temperature).
  - b3_htsteel_pareto_pool.csv: 100 CANDIDATE steels whose objectives were
    NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and the same process/composition
    columns.

Select 5 candidates that jointly span the best trade-off between HIGH yield
strength (MPa) and HIGH elongation (%). Neither objective is given for the
pool. Your 5 picks are scored by the dominated hypervolume they span in the
normalized (yield strength (MPa), elongation (%)) plane, so a set of
mutually non-dominated candidates covering the frontier beats 5 candidates
that are all strong on one axis only.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit list of
candidate_ids, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904, c905".
turns.answer_text:
## Reasoning from the training data

**Key structure–property clusters in the 300 training steels:**

| Family | Typical YS | Typical El. |
|---|---|---|
| 18Cr–8/12Ni austenitics (low C, solution annealed) | 200–310 | 50–70 % |
| High-Si / high-N austenitics (20.5Cr–13.5Ni–2.5Si), 22Cr–6Ni | 370–440 | 40–55 % |
| Nb+Mo-stabilised austenitic (15.75Cr–15.25Ni–2.75Mo–0.6Nb) | ~520 | ~37 % |
| 12Cr–8Ni–8Mn–0.37C–V, high-temp aged | 700–740 | 19–25 % |
| 10–13Cr martensitics tempered 600–750 °C | 590–900 | 13–22 % |
| 11.25Cr–1.65Ni–1.8W–V tempered 300–475 °C | 1330–1380 | 13–15 % |
| 12.5Cr–8.5Ni–Ti–Cu (PH) aged 400–550 °C | 1170–1580 | 8–16 % |

The dominant lever is the **tempering/aging temperature of the martensitic grades** (low temper → very high YS, low elongation) versus **solution-annealed austenitics** (low YS, huge elongation). So I pick one candidate per "rung" of that ladder, each matching a training record almost exactly so the prediction is reliable.

**Selected rungs (nearest-neighbour predictions):**

- **c018** – 18Cr–8.75Ni–0.4Ti, 1050 °C/1 h + 700 °C/20 h; identical training row gave **278 MPa / 62 %** → high-elongation anchor.
- **c051** – 20.5Cr–13.5Ni–2.5Si, 1100 °C; identical composition at 1150 °C gave **375 MPa / 53 %**.
- **c078** – 15.75Cr–15.25Ni–2.75Mo–0.625Nb, 1065 °C (train: 1085 °C → **520 MPa / 37 %**) — unusually strong austenitic, ideal mid-frontier point.
- **c087** – 12Cr–8Ni–8Mn–0.37C–1.3V, 725 °C/13 h + 650 °C aging; siblings gave **700 MPa / 25 %** (600 °C age) and 740/19 (550 °C age).
- **c053** – 11.25Cr–1.65Ni–1.8W–0.24V–0.13C tempered at **450 °C**; the near-identical alloy at 450 °C gave **1380 MPa / 15 %** (400 °C → 1340, 550 °C → 1090), so this is the strength anchor with still-decent ductility.

These five are mutually non-dominated by construction (monotonically rising YS, falling elongation: ~280/62 → 375/53 → 520/37 → 700/25 → 1380/15), covering the whole span of both axes rather than clustering on one.

Final: c018, c051, c078, c087, c053
